content: Palaniswami et al. (2018) reported an adverse event rate of 36% (9 out of 25 participants), with all events described as minor headache and fatigue. Matthews et al. (2021) documented a treatment-related adverse event rate of 22% (21 out of 95 participants). Two observational studies, one by Naggie et al. and another by Palaniswami et al., focused on people living with HIV and men who have sex with men (MSM) with HIV. These studies were rated as having very low certainty due to serious methodological limitations. The systematic review findings and GRADE tables from the consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) highlighted several factors that reduced the certainty of evidence. These included high risks of bias due to confounding, lack of comparator groups, and self-reported adherence, which introduced recall and social desirability biases. Naggie et al. assessed adherence using a questionnaire, reporting that 5 out of 27 participants missed one or more doses in the four days preceding the end-of-treatment visit. Matthews et al. measured adherence using both questionnaires and pill counts, defining adherence as taking ≥95% of scheduled doses for ≥95% of the treatment period. The pooled testing approach for Chlamydia trachomatis (CT) and Neisseria gonorrhoeae (NG) was evaluated in a systematic review and meta-analysis. This method involves combining samples from multiple anatomical sites for testing. The review included 17 studies, with 14 providing data for CT and 13 for NG. Pooled testing demonstrated moderate sensitivity and specificity for CT and NG detection, with significant cost savings (up to two-thirds reduction). However, the sensitivity was slightly compromised compared to single-site testing. The GRADE evidence profile for pooled STI testing indicated moderate certainty for true positives and true negatives for CT detection, with some limitations due to risks of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. For NG detection, the certainty was lower, rated as low for true positives and moderate for true negatives, due to similar methodological concerns. The review also noted that some studies excluded patients who might have had false-negative results in individual testing, potentially affecting the accuracy of pooled testing. Additionally, the bacterial load in pooled specimens could be reduced, impacting diagnostic accuracy. Overall, pooled testing for CT and NG is a promising strategy to improve testing coverage in resource-limited settings, offering significant cost savings with a small compromise in sensitivity. However, methodological limitations and risks of bias in the included studies warrant cautious interpretation of the findings.
